paragraphs: First examine the actual occupation: install, test, maintain, and repair electromechanical or robotic equipment, read drawings, use test instruments, and record deviations. Typical reviewable outputs include assembly and test records, fault trees, measurement results, repair recommendations, and safety handovers. Paper exercises must not energize equipment, disassemble machines, or bypass interlocks. In applicable U.S. general industry settings, trained and authorized personnel perform actual testing, repair, and safety release under 29 CFR 1910.147 and employer/equipment procedures; check applicable rules separately for other industries or jurisdictions.

Safe trial materials (all fictional): fictional packaging line M-2, already locked out and tagged, with the exercise using only paper records. 24V signal table: S1 door interlock expected 0V, logged 24V; S2 emergency stop circuit expected 24V, logged 24V; S3 air pressure permissive expected 24V, logged 0V; S4 motor overload expected 0V, logged 0V. Timeline: 10:00 shutdown, 10:05 lockout/tagout performed, 10:12 logs exported. Mechanical records say “guard door closed”; electrical records say “S1 still high.” Rule: only mark differences, without judging whether energization is permitted. Task: list matching/mismatching signals, items requiring verification about mechanical state and signal relationships, required offline verification, and an issue report summary.

Reference reasoning: based only on the table, S2/S4 match expectations, while S1/S3 differ. The 10:12 log is later than the 10:05 lockout/tagout, but this cannot establish that all energy sources and isolation points have been verified. “Door closed” and S1 high constitute a semantic conflict only when drawing definitions, inverted logic, and sampling times agree. Do not change the existing lockout/tagout state. First verify isolation and de-energization, drawing/I/O versions, signal definitions, and log times; authorized personnel then perform offline measurements under applicable regulations and employer/equipment procedures.

Suitability signals: willing to take on production sites, noise and hazardous energy, downtime pressure, shifts, and learning across mechanical/electrical/control systems, while separating evidence, unknowns, professional judgment, and authority. Caution signals: liking only paper organization while rejecting actual settings, training, and responsibility.

O*NET17-3024 electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians: operate, test, maintain, and adjust automated, servo, or electromechanical equipment, and may assist with robot design and testing; 29 tasks, RCI, Zone3. Education feedback: 32% postsecondary certificate, 30% associate degree, and 11% bachelor’s degree. This is a U.S. survey, rather than statutory thresholds.

entries: Actual inputs include mechanical and electrical drawings, equipment specifications, I/O and control logic, operating and alarm logs, measurement results, maintenance history, work orders, and lockout/tagout status.

paragraphs: Typical process: assemble and install against drawings, perform safety isolation, test and calibrate with instruments, locate mechanical/electrical/hydraulic/pneumatic problems, repair or replace components, retest and record results, then complete a safety handover.

Main outputs: assembly and test records, fault trees, measurement results, repair recommendations, and safety handovers. Each deliverable should state evidence, limitations, responsible persons, and next steps.

Key judgments: align mechanical states, signal definitions, measurement times, and drawing versions; develop and eliminate fault hypotheses, select safe test steps, and determine when engineers, suppliers, or safety leads must intervene.

Collaboration and authority: collaborate with engineers, production, maintenance, safety, and suppliers. Trained technicians may perform approved site tasks; corresponding authorized parties decide design changes, interlock bypasses, energization, and safety release.

Environment and tools: manufacturing sites and offices/laboratories, with possible exposure to noise, moving equipment, and electrical and pneumatic/hydraulic energy; use multimeters, oscilloscopes/test equipment, precision measuring tools, machining and welding tools, and maintenance systems.

Confirm hazardous energy control, drawing and I/O versions, instruments and units, and post-repair retesting under actual equipment safety procedures; check Subpart S separately for electrical exposure. Do not describe 147 as governing all testing or safety release.
Robotics technologists focus more on robot controllers, end effectors, and automation cells; electromechanical technologists cover broader mechanical, electrical, and control interfaces.
Aerospace engineers handle system design and engineering analysis; technologists assemble, adjust, and record against approved drawings, without replacing design signing.
Electrical engineers define circuits and electrical safety requirements; electromechanical technologists provide measurement, assembly, and fault records.
Electronics engineers focus on electronic system design; electromechanical technologists also handle interactions between mechanisms, sensors, and actuators.

Editorial trials: organize drawing/I/O text, maintenance logs, and measurement data in approved environments, generating summaries or missing-item prompts. Instruments and machining tools are not objects that can be directly handed to AI for organization; recheck outputs against original materials.
